title: Whiplash — a Cinematic Story Edit
description: Build tension with dialogue, bold captions and an accelerating finish. Adapt the workflow to your own footage.
promptSource: Adaptable prompt derived from the saved Whiplash edit’s source inspection, timeline, caption layouts and production records. The shown video was made in an earlier reference-reconstruction run, not generated by this new prompt. Film: Whiplash (2014). Music: Grant Steller, Every Living Breathing Moment. Source footage and music are not part of the open-source toolkit.
prompt:
Use Video Use to turn my supplied or licensed footage into a cinematic story edit. Carry forward the subject, audience, format, length and level of involvement already established in this conversation. If no length is set, aim for 45–60 seconds. Adapt the editing language of this example to my material; choose new shots and words that fit my story.

Inspect the footage and transcribe the useful dialogue before choosing cuts. Find a clear subject, a goal, an obstacle and a payoff. Use only events and spoken words supported by the source. Open with a compelling line or visible action, hold long enough to understand the stakes, then alternate effort, resistance and reactions. Give the strongest setback a little breathing room. Build toward a final 6–10 seconds of shorter, energetic shots that show the payoff. Keep that final burst mostly free of text. Preserve the meaning of dialogue and the order of any process being demonstrated.

Use mostly clean hard cuts. Let expressions, eyelines and movement motivate each cut; save the fastest cutting for the finish. Keep natural motion unless a deliberate speed change improves a specific moment. Use a restrained, high-contrast grade with believable skin tones and consistent shots within each setting.

Add selective, bold, uppercase slab-serif captions in white, with a few important words in red. Build short phrases in sync with actual speech, placing them in available negative space. Leave uncaptained passages for the images to breathe. Keep text readable and clear of faces, hands and important action throughout the cue. If the footage supports it, use one brief isolated-subject-on-black moment at the emotional peak, then return to the scene. Omit it if a clean moving matte cannot be achieved.

Edit dialogue and music on separate timelines. Choose a licensed or original track whose changing intensity supports the story. Align key transitions to its actual phrases and accents rather than forcing every cut onto a fixed beat grid. Keep dialogue clear, music continuous across picture cuts, and sound effects sparse and motivated. Avoid clipped words, cut clicks and an abruptly truncated music tail.

Render the agreed format with current Video Use tools and retain an editable EDL, caption timing, fonts, audio decisions and source credits. Check the encoded cut boundaries, speech alignment, moving text/subject collisions, first frame and final hold; decode the complete file and verify both audio and picture duration. Follow the existing involvement mode, including a short approval snippet before the full edit in hands-on mode.

title: Dead Air Removal
description: Remove pauses and repeated speech from a camera unboxing.
prompt: Tighten this unboxing footage into a natural 12–15 second clip. Find one useful complete thought about the camera, then remove hesitations, repeated words, long pauses, and time spent fumbling with packaging. Keep the speaker’s real voice and meaning. Use clean cuts and only a small change in crop when it helps cover a jump. Keep the product visible. No music, flashy transitions, title cards, or decorative overlays.

title: Detail Crop
description: Select clear product views from a long unboxing.
prompt: Turn this raw camera unboxing into a clear 12–15 second product showcase. Skip the packaging struggle and find three genuinely useful views of the camera: the full product, a close detail being handled, and a satisfying finished view. Cut when the hands move naturally and use careful close crops to show what matters. Hold each detail long enough to understand it. Keep real handling sounds; omit incomplete speech. No invented features, music, graphic frames, or unnecessary text.

title: Process Cutdown
description: Condense packaging and setup into a short reveal.
prompt: Turn the slow box-opening and setup in this unboxing footage into a satisfying 12–15 second reveal. Show a brief sealed-box or wrapped-product moment, keep only the decisive opening and assembly actions, and finish on the camera fully revealed and ready to use. Remove searching, repeated handling, empty hands, and long gaps. Preserve the real order of events and keep clean original handling sounds. No added music, fake product facts, title cards, or flashy transitions.

title: Vertical Reframe
description: Reframe a product demonstration for a vertical short.
prompt: Make a useful 12–15 second vertical short from this widescreen camera-unboxing footage. Choose one complete product demonstration with an actual reveal or useful takeaway. Cut the idle handling and pauses, reframe each shot to keep the camera and the demonstrator’s hands visible, and move the crop only when the product moves. Keep any included speech intact and add clean accurate phrase captions within safe margins. Use the speaker’s own voice and real sounds. No blurred background bars, stretching, fake words, music, or decorative transitions.

title: Speed Ramp
description: Acceleration, a slow-motion peak, and cuts that follow the action.
prompt: Use only the supplied Tears of Steel source video to make a 12-second widescreen action edit called Velocity. Inspect the source first and choose four genuinely energetic shots with clear camera or subject motion; avoid dialogue-only holds and credits. Build a readable arc: 0–2s an intriguing moving detail, 2–5s three escalating action cuts, 5–8s one hero movement that eases from 100% to 45% speed for its peak then accelerates to 220%, 8–11s a decisive payoff, 11–12s a clean visual finish. Cut on matching movement directions and use two 6-frame whip transitions only where source motion supports them. Add a single 6% punch-in on the strongest impact. Preserve sharp faces and edges; use frame sampling if interpolation bends objects. Keep original environmental sound where useful, add a restrained original percussive pulse and two synchronized impacts, and duck the pulse under any retained intelligible speech. No stock footage, no new generated scenes, no full-screen captions, and no random flash/glitch effects. Deliver one polished 1920x1080 H264 MP4 with intentional crops, no stretched image, plus source timecodes and an edit decision list. The edit must still clearly communicate acceleration and payoff when muted.

title: Freeze Frame Poster
description: A moving shot becomes an editorial poster, then returns to motion.
prompt: Turn the same supplied Tears of Steel source into a 12-second widescreen moving film poster. Choose one continuous shot with at least 6 seconds of usable motion with a clear expressive character or striking mechanical silhouette. Start full-screen in motion for 2.5s; stop precisely on the strongest pose with a clean 8-frame camera ease, then animate the frozen image into a large offset rectangular crop over a warm ivory background. Reveal three small close-up tiles from that exact same frame—an eye or face detail, a mechanical detail, and a texture—with precise staggered slides. Use bold condensed black typography reading 'A MOMENT / IN MOTION', one small burnt-orange index '01', and thin alignment rules. Keep the frozen hero recognizably photographic and let scale/position supply depth; do not attempt a rough automatic cutout. Hold the completed editorial poster from 6.5–9s, then resolve the tiles into the full original frame and resume its source motion from the exact held frame for the final 3s. Use restrained dry camera clicks and the source ambience. No footage beyond the one source. Deliver 1920x1080 H264 MP4, crisp type, generous margins, no unreadable microtext, source timecodes, and the edit decision list.

title: Animated Split Screen
description: Three views share the frame and exchange emphasis.
prompt: Create a 12-second 1920x1080 widescreen editorial split-screen film using only the same supplied Tears of Steel source. Pick one short sequence with a clear subject and useful wide, medium, and close-up views. Open as one uninterrupted full-width shot for 1.5s. Slide two thin cream dividers into place over 0.5s to reveal a deliberate 25% / 50% / 25% triptych: left is an environment or gesture detail, center is the hero action, right is a face or mechanical detail. Use different source moments or crops, never three identical copies; align the most important actions to meet at 5s. At 6s smoothly transfer the center panel's dominance to the right by resizing the panels over 12 frames, maintaining every subject's framing. At 9s make a clean synchronized match cut across all three panels. From 10.5–12s expand the strongest panel to full screen and finish on a satisfying moving frame. White balance all panels coherently and use warm off-white 5px gutters, no rounded app-card styling. Retain a continuous source ambience with gentle edit accents. No captions except small optional '01', '02', '03' outside faces. Deliver the MP4 and exact crop/timecode decisions. Every panel must visibly contribute a different view.

title: Cinematic Grade
description: A moving comparison reveals cool shadows and controlled warm highlights.
prompt: Create a 10-second cinematic color transformation from the same supplied Tears of Steel source. In the final 2.5s show a concise moving 50/50 original-versus-grade comparison with small crisp 'SOURCE' and 'AFTER DARK' labels in the lower safe area.
